newsitem.title: USA: Cable TV carriers eye rate increases.
newsitem.headline: Cable TV carriers eye rate increases.

text.p: Some of the nation's largest cable operators are preparing to raise prices next year, a move that could send subscribers flocking to direct satellite sytems.

Telecommunications Inc., the nation's biggest cable operator, on Thursday announced plans to raise basic rates an average of 6 percent to 7 percent next year, and Time Warner Inc.'s cable division said Friday it plans similar increases in the new year.
Cable companies blame the price increases on higher programming costs and massive investments to upgrade cable networks in the face of growing competition from satellite delivery systems.
But some experts claim the cable industry is merely raising rates to boost revenues.

"The story is the cable companies have a monopoly over pay TV," said Andrew Schwartzman of Media Access Project, a consumer rights group. "If the competition was effective, cable companies would not be raising rates. They're doing it because they can."

Indeed, with only 4 million subscribers natiowide, compared with 65 million cable customers, direct broadcast systems have a long way to go before they can challenge the cable industry for control of the nation's airwaves.
However, in recent months, cable companies have started to take notice of direct broadcast satellite systems (DBS) such as Hughes Electronics Corp's DirectTV.

"While we do believe it is becomming a bigger factor than it was ... the impact of DBS in most of our areas is primarly in those areas that are more rural and may be lower channel capacities," said a spokesman for Time Warner Cable.
"It is a business and it is growing, but so far it has not taken significant numbers of customers from us," he added.

The growing popularity of satellite systems, which provide up to 200 channels of movies, news, music and sports in digital sound, has caught many experts by surprise. When the devices were first demonstrated a few years ago, few cable operators believed customers would spend upwards of $600 for an 18-inch dish.
But as dish prices have fallen below $200, the number of subscribers has risen sharply. Last month, DirecTV, signed up customer number 2 million, doubling the company's client base in just 11 months.
The rise of satellite systems has prompted cable companies to rethink their strategy and focus on keeping customers.
At TCI, officials believe cancellations have slowed and the company has started to win back some of the 70,000 cable subscribers who left last summer.
TCI, which has 14 million subscribers, posted net gains of 10,000 to 15,000 customers in September and October and further gains were continuing in November.

TCI officials attributed the bulk of the cancellations to rate increases earlier in the year under a settlement with the Federal Communications Commission rather than competition from satellite systems.
According to the government, cable rates are up 7.3 percent for first 10 months through October, more than twice the rate of inflation.

Time Warner, which has about 12.1 million customers, said it needs to raise rates to pay for high-cost programs and expensive system upgrades. Starting in January, it expects to increase cable rates by an average of about 7 percent.
Currently, the average Time Warner customer pays about $35 a month for service, which includes basic channels and at least one premium channel.
